cutting.intro: Trim lightly to keep growth clean and balanced.
bullets: Every 1–2 weeks, remove spent leaves, damaged parts, and weak leggy stems to improve light reach and airflow.
Use clean, sharp scissors or pruners, and disinfect blades before and after cutting to reduce disease spread.

support.intro: Check supports weekly as Cannabis sativa gains height and weight.
bullets: Inspect ties for tightness and loosen any that press into stems.
Make sure stakes or trellises stay firm in the potting mix.
Guide new growth onto support every 7–10 days as needed.

aeration.intro: Loosen the topsoil every 2–3 weeks if it starts to crust or harden.
bullets: Use a small stick or fork to gently loosen the top 2–3 cm (1 in) without disturbing roots.
Compaction is likely if water sits on the surface or drains unevenly.
Wipe dusty leaves gently with a soft, damp cloth and support each leaf to avoid tearing.
Remove fallen debris and rinse the pot rim and saucer to improve light capture, reduce pest shelter, and keep the plant tidy.

humidity.intro: Extra humidity support is usually only needed in dry indoor air.
bullets: Check weekly and use a pebble tray or humidifier if humidity drops below 40%; dry leaf edges can signal air that is too dry.

mulching.intro: Refresh the top-dressing every 3–4 weeks if the surface layer thins.
bullets: Use a thin 1–2 cm (0.5–1 in) layer of clean straw, coco chips, or compost.
This helps hold moisture evenly and buffers root-zone temperature swings.

watering.intro: Water marijuana when early dryness appears.
bullets: Every 3–5 days, water when the top 2–3 cm (1 in) feels dry or leaves show slight droop.
Soak the soil fully until excess drains, then empty the saucer and avoid standing water.
Do not top up small amounts too often, which keeps roots too wet and invites rot.
For marijuana, apply a balanced NPK fertilizer every 7–14 days at 1/2-strength during vegetative growth.
Water the soil first if dry, then feed evenly to moist soil to reduce root stress.
Pause or reduce feeding if growth slows, and avoid overfeeding, which can cause tip burn and salt buildup.

repotting.intro: Check regularly for signs the pot is too small.
bullets: Every 2–3 weeks, inspect for roots at drainage holes, slowed growth, or water running straight through the mix.
If needed, move up 5–10 cm (2–4 in) wider than the current pot to avoid excess wet soil.
Lift and turn leaves to view undersides, check the stem base, and look into drainage holes for escaping roots.
Take follow-up action if you find root crowding, soft stem tissue, pests, or blocked drainage.

monitoring.intro: Do a quick health scan every 2–3 days.
bullets: Look at leaf color and texture, new growth, surface moisture, and any pest activity.
If something looks off, adjust watering or light first and isolate the plant for closer follow-up if needed.

careDetails.aboutPlant:
Cannabis sativa is an annual flowering herb in the Cannabaceae family. It usually grows upright with fast, vigorous growth, deeply divided leaves, and a strong response to seasonal light changes.

Native to eastern Asia, it is now grown widely in many regions through long cultivation. Its need for intense light, steady moisture, and good airflow can affect how easy care for marijuana feels indoors or outdoors.

It generally prefers rich, well-draining loamy soil and consistent moisture without waterlogging. Growers often find that light levels and overwatering are the main challenges.

careAdvice.title: Gentle air movement
careAdvice.description: Use an oscillating fan to keep light air moving around the canopy, which helps reduce stagnant moisture, strengthens stems, and lowers the risk of fungal problems indoors.

careAdvice.title: Canopy training
careAdvice.description: Bend and tie flexible stems outward early to create a flatter, more even canopy so lower growth receives better light, a standard practice when growing marijuana under lamps.

careAdvice.title: Branch support
careAdvice.description: Add soft plant ties, stakes, or a trellis before heavy flowering so branches do not split or lean once buds gain weight.

careAdvice.title: Sticky trap checks
careAdvice.description: Place yellow sticky traps near the pot and inspect leaf undersides weekly to catch fungus gnats, whiteflies, or mites early, which is especially useful when caring for marijuana indoors.

careAdvice.title: Dark-period control
careAdvice.description: During flowering, prevent stray light from timers, windows, or nearby rooms during the 12-hour dark period because interruptions can stress plants and disrupt bud development.

soil.intro: Cannabis sativa needs a loose, airy, organic-rich loamy mix.
bullets: Use loam blended with compost or worm castings for structure and steady nutrient supply.
Add 20–30% perlite or vermiculite to improve aeration and help excess water drain quickly.
Keep pH at 6.0–6.5 for nutrient uptake and avoid dense, compacted, waterlogged mixes.
Do not use heavy clay or poorly drained media that stay wet around the roots.

water.intro: Cannabis sativa prefers even moisture in fast-draining soil.
bullets: Water when the top 2–3 cm (1 in) of soil feels dry, rather than by a fixed schedule; in warm weather this is often about every 4 days.
Reduce watering in cooler, slower-growth periods, and increase only when heat, wind, or rapid growth dries the root zone faster.
Poor drainage and constant wet soil can cause drooping, yellowing, and root rot, while dry soil leads to wilting, leaf curl, and crisp edges.

soilPH.intro: Soil pH strongly affects Cannabis sativa nutrient uptake and root health.
bullets: Keep pH at 6.0–6.5 in slightly acidic soil for steady growth.
Test with a soil pH meter or kit; raise pH with lime, lower it with sulfur or pH-adjusted water.
Wrong pH can cause nutrient lock-out, chlorosis, slow growth, and weak stems.

pruning.intro: Pruning helps Cannabis sativa stay open, balanced, and productive.
bullets: Trim in the vegetative stage or early flowering, not during late flowering.
Remove dead, damaged, or crowded lower shoots and weak interior growth.
Use clean scissors or pruners, making neat cuts above a node to guide shape.
Careful thinning improves airflow, light reach, and can support more even flowering.
It tolerates somewhat dry air, but sustained levels below 40% can slow growth and crisp leaf edges.
Humidity stress shows as curling leaves, brown tips, and unusually fast soil drying.
Raise humidity with a humidifier, grouped plants, or a pebble tray, while keeping airflow steady.

sunlight.intro: Cannabis sativa grows best with long, direct sun exposure through the main growing season.
bullets: Provide 6–8 hours of direct sun outdoors; vegetative plants grow fastest with 18 hours under grow lights, while flowering needs about 12 hours.
Partial shade is tolerated for short periods, but morning sun and full afternoon sun produce stronger growth than filtered light or deep shade.
Marijuana becomes lanky in low light, with smaller flowers; in extreme summer heat, intense reflected sun can scorch leaves and dry soil too quickly.

container.intro: This species is well suited to container growing.
bullets: Use a pot with several drainage holes so excess water leaves fast after each watering.
Choose a 30–50 cm (12–20 in) wide, deep container to support root mass and reduce rapid drying.
A heavier plastic or fabric pot with a broad base helps steady tall, top-heavy Cannabis sativa plants.

placement.intro: Placement depends on light strength, airflow, and temperature stability.
bullets: Indoors, marijuana does best under grow lights or near a south-facing window; outdoors, use a bright, sheltered site.
Allow 45–60 cm (18–24 in) between plants or pots so air moves freely around foliage.
Avoid cold drafts, heating vents, and intense midday sun outdoors in very hot climates.

fertilizer.intro: Cannabis sativa benefits from steady feeding during active growth.
bullets: Use a balanced NPK fertilizer, compost, or a light slow-release blend in loamy soil.
Feed every 1–2 weeks in the growing season at 1/2 strength to avoid salt buildup.
Reduce feeding sharply in winter or dormancy, especially in low light or cooler conditions.

winterCare.intro: This annual is frost-sensitive and does not overwinter outdoors in cold climates.
bullets: Move container plants indoors before temperatures drop below 10°C (50°F).
Keep roots insulated with mulch if finishing the season outside in mild areas.
Avoid freezing exposure, which quickly damages stems, leaves, and flowers.

propagation.intro: Propagation is most often done from seed for reliable establishment.
bullets: Sow seeds in spring in a warm medium at 20–25°C (68–77°F).
Keep the mix lightly moist, not wet, with bright light after sprouting.
Use a loose, well-draining seed-starting mix and shallow sowing at 1–2 cm (0.4–0.8 in).
Transplant seedlings carefully once they have several true leaves and firm roots.

temperature.intro: Warm conditions support steady growth and reliable flowering.
bullets: Aim for 68–86°F (20–30°C) during active growth; plants usually perform best with warm days and slightly cooler nights.
Growth slows below 60°F (16°C), and Cannabis sativa is highly sensitive to frost; prolonged exposure near 32°F (0°C) can kill tissues.
Heat above 90°F (32°C) can reduce vigor and increase water stress, especially in midsummer, so some afternoon relief helps in very hot regions.

repottingAndTransplanting.intro: Move plants before roots become cramped to keep growth steady.
bullets: Repot or transplant in spring or early vegetative growth, before heavy flowering starts.
Signs include roots circling the pot, roots from drainage holes, or slowed growth.
Container plants often need 1 size up once or twice during the season.
Water before moving, keep the root ball intact, and transplant into moist loamy soil.

facts.text: This species was formally described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753, but it had already been cultivated for a very long time for fiber, seed oil, and food. Its species name, sativa, means cultivated.
facts.title: Ancient cultivated species

facts.text: Many plants produce either male or female flowers on separate individuals, which makes the species notable among common annual crops. Some cultivated forms can also show monoecious or intersex traits.
facts.title: Usually dioecious growth

facts.text: It belongs to the Cannabaceae family, the same family as hops, Humulus lupulus. This relationship is reflected in shared botanical traits within the group.
facts.title: Cannabaceae relative

interestingFacts.didYouKnow: Archaeological evidence shows that this species has been used by people since ancient times across multiple regions, making it one of the oldest multipurpose cultivated plants known.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Spider mites
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Rinse foliage thoroughly, especially leaf undersides, and raise humidity to 40–60% if conditions are too dry. Use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with full coverage, and repeat every 5–7 days as needed.
pestsAndDiseases.description: These tiny arachnids feed on leaf tissue and often become severe in warm, dry grow rooms. Symptoms include fine webbing, pale speckling, and gradual leaf decline.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Powdery mildew
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Remove affected leaves, improve air circulation, and avoid wetting foliage late in the day. Treat early with potassium bicarbonate or a suitable horticultural fungicide labeled for edible crops, following label directions carefully.
pestsAndDiseases.description: This disease appears as a white, dusty coating on leaves and stems and spreads quickly where airflow is poor. It can reduce vigor and interfere with healthy flower development.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Botrytis bud rot
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Cut out infected flowers immediately and discard them away from the growing area. Keep humidity near 40–50% during flowering, maintain strong airflow, and avoid overcrowding plants.
pestsAndDiseases.description: This disease affects dense flowers, especially under high humidity during flowering. Symptoms include browning within buds, gray mold, and soft, decaying tissue.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Fungus gnats
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Let the top 2–3 cm (1 in) of soil dry slightly between waterings while keeping overall moisture balanced. Use yellow sticky traps for adults and apply beneficial nematodes or Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis for larvae.
pestsAndDiseases.description: These insects are common in consistently moist potting mixes, and their larvae feed on organic matter and fine roots. Symptoms include weak growth, yellowing, and small dark flies around the soil surface.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Hemp russet mites
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Isolate affected plants, remove badly damaged growth, and inspect new material carefully before placing it nearby. Use sulfur products in vegetative growth only where appropriate, or a horticultural oil labeled for mite control, and repeat treatments as directed.
pestsAndDiseases.description: These microscopic mites are strongly associated with this crop and can be hard to detect early. Symptoms include curled leaves, bronzing, stunted growth, and damaged flowers.

faqs.answer: Ja. Es wächst gut in Containern, wenn der Topf eine starke Drainage und genügend Wurzelraum hat. Schnelles Wachstum kann dazu führen, dass es im Topf eingeklemmt wird, daher sollte die Topfgröße erhöht werden, wenn die Wurzeln das Substrat ausfüllen.
